posGateway.title: The POS terminal cannot reach the internet

complaint.message: At the new branch the POS terminal cannot reach the internet, so we cannot take card payments.

hints: In the POS terminal's Terminal tab, first check its IP settings with ipconfig, then ping its default gateway.
Compare the "Default gateway" address in the POS terminal's Settings tab with the modem's LAN address (192.168.10.1).
Change the POS terminal's gateway from 192.168.1.1 to 192.168.10.1. The IP address 192.168.10.20 and the mask 255.255.255.0 can stay as they are.

explanation.whatHappened: The default gateway entered manually (statically) on the POS terminal, 192.168.1.1, was the modem address of the old branch. Because the POS terminal is on the 192.168.10.x network, that address was outside its own subnet, so the terminal had no way out to the internet. The devices on the same network that get their address via DHCP received the correct gateway (192.168.10.1) automatically, so they had no problem.
explanation.realLife: This happens very often when a POS terminal, printer or PC is removed from one branch and moved to another with its old static settings: the device shows up on the local network but cannot reach the internet or the payment system. To prevent it, reset the IP settings before moving a device, use DHCP whenever possible (with a DHCP reservation on the modem if a fixed address is needed), and keep each branch's IP plan (network address, default gateway, DNS) documented.
explanation.interviewAnswer: I start with the physical layer: is the POS terminal powered on, is the cable plugged in, is the switch port's link light on. Then I check the IP address, subnet mask and default gateway with ipconfig; here I see that the terminal is 192.168.10.20 but its gateway is 192.168.1.1, which is on a different network. I confirm this by pinging the gateway and correct the gateway to the modem's LAN address, 192.168.10.1. Then I verify internet access by pinging 8.8.8.8 and finally use nslookup to check that the payment server's name resolves.

printerDhcp.title: The printer has disappeared

complaint.message: The printer worked yesterday, but today nobody can print.

hints: Look up the printer address saved on the PCs (Info tab) and ping it. Then check the printer's own address.
Select the printer and look at its current address in the Info tab: is it the same as 192.168.1.150, the address the PCs expect? The printer gets its address automatically via DHCP.

Set the printer's IP address assignment to Manual (static): IP 192.168.1.150, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 192.168.1.1. Both PCs will then find the printer again. In real life you should also exclude this address from the modem's DHCP range or assign it to the printer as a DHCP reservation.

explanation.whatHappened: The printer was getting its address automatically via DHCP. When its lease expired and it requested an address again, the modem gave it 192.168.1.153 instead of 192.168.1.150. The PCs were still looking for the printer at the old address, 192.168.1.150, so they could not send any print jobs.
explanation.realLife: Every device that other devices find by its address, such as a printer, camera or video recorder, should have a fixed address. The permanent fix is to give the printer a static IP or to create a DHCP reservation for the printer's MAC address on the modem, not to change the printer address on every PC one by one, because the problem comes back the next time the printer's address changes. When you assign a static address, choosing one outside the range the modem hands out automatically, or excluding it from that range, prevents two devices from getting the same address. Documenting the fixed addresses in a list also makes the job easier.
explanation.interviewAnswer: First I do the physical checks: is the printer on, is an error light lit, is the network cable plugged in. Then I find the address the PCs use for the printer and ping it; when there is no reply, I check the printer's current address in the network settings on its own display or on a printed network configuration page. Seeing that the printer got a new address via DHCP (192.168.1.153), I fix it permanently by giving the printer the address the PCs expect, 192.168.1.150, as a static address, or by creating a DHCP reservation for that address on the modem. Finally I ping the printer from every PC and print a test page to confirm the problem is solved.

cameraSubnet.title: No video from Camera 3

complaint.message: The video recorder shows no picture from camera number 3.

hints: Ping all three cameras from the video recorder's Terminal tab and find the one that does not reply.
Camera 3 appears to be powered on and cabled; compare the IP address and gateway in Camera 3's Settings tab with those of the other cameras.
Change Camera 3's IP address from 192.168.0.64 to 192.168.1.63 and its gateway to 192.168.1.1 (the mask stays 255.255.255.0).

explanation.whatHappened: Camera 3 had reverted to its factory settings and started up with the manufacturer's default address, 192.168.0.64. The video recorder and the other cameras were on the 192.168.1.x network; the recorder was looking for the camera at 192.168.1.63, so it could not find it. Cabling and power were fine; the only problem was that the address was on a different network.
explanation.realLife: Cameras can revert to factory settings after a power outage, a reset button held down too long or a firmware update, and then start up with their default address. To prevent trouble, keep a list of every camera's IP and MAC address, label the switch ports, and reconfigure a reset camera with the same address. Backing up the camera configuration after installation makes reconfiguring a reset camera faster. Putting the cameras in their own VLAN is a separate security and organization measure that has nothing to do with this fault.
explanation.interviewAnswer: First I do the physical checks: is the camera's PoE light on, is the switch port active, is the cable intact. I ping the faulty camera's address from the video recorder, and when there is no reply I look at the camera's own IP settings. Seeing that it is running on its factory default address, 192.168.0.64, which is on a different network, I correct its IP address to 192.168.1.63 and its gateway to 192.168.1.1. Finally I ping it again from the recorder and check that the video comes through.

kitchenVlan.title: Orders do not reach the kitchen

complaint.message: Orders entered on the POS terminal do not show up on the kitchen display.

hints: Ping the kitchen display's address (192.168.10.30) from the POS terminal. If the IP settings look correct, look for the problem on the switch port the cable is plugged into.
Check the switch's port settings: the POS terminal is connected to Fa0/2, the kitchen display to Fa0/3. Are both ports in the same VLAN?
On the switch, set port Fa0/3 to access mode in VLAN 10. The phone on the guest network belongs in VLAN 20; leave it as it is.

explanation.whatHappened: Switch port Fa0/3, where the kitchen display is plugged in, was assigned to the guest network VLAN 20 instead of the business network VLAN 10. Although the display's IP settings were correct, the switch put it in the guest network, so the POS terminal could not find a display it assumed was on the same network. Once the port was set to VLAN 10, both were back on the same network.
explanation.realLife: In businesses that keep the guest Wi-Fi in a separate VLAN, this problem is common when someone plugs a cable into another port or a port setting is changed by mistake. To prevent it, label switch ports and wall outlets with the VLAN they belong to, document the port-to-VLAN table and back up the switch configuration. Putting the guest network in its own VLAN separates the two networks; the fault is not the separation itself but the port being assigned to the wrong VLAN. A VLAN alone is not enough, though: to make sure guests cannot reach business devices at all, you also need an access rule on the router (an ACL or a firewall rule).
explanation.interviewAnswer: First I do the physical checks: is the kitchen display on, is its cable plugged in, is the switch port's link light on. Then I look at both devices' network settings (ipconfig on the POS terminal, the display's own settings menu) and confirm that the IP address, mask and gateway are correct and in the same network. If the POS terminal still cannot ping the display even though the settings are correct, I check whether both devices are in the same VLAN on the switch; here I find that Fa0/3, the display's port, is in VLAN 20 and change it to VLAN 10. Finally I ping the display from the POS terminal again, confirm the fix with a test order and check that the guest network still reaches the internet.

wrongDns.title: The internet works, but no website opens

complaint.message: They say the internet is working, but no website opens on my computer.

hints: From the accounting PC, ping the address 8.8.8.8 first, then the name google.com. If one works and the other does not, try nslookup google.com.
On the accounting PC, check the DNS server address with ipconfig /all and ping that address. Compare it with the DNS setting of the Sales PC, which works.
Change the accounting PC's DNS server from 192.168.1.254 to 192.168.1.1 (the modem). 8.8.8.8 would also work as the DNS server.

explanation.whatHappened: The accounting PC's DNS server had been entered manually as 192.168.1.254, the address of an old modem that is no longer on the network. The PC could reach the internet (pings to 8.8.8.8 worked), but it could not translate website names into IP addresses, so no website opened. Once the DNS server was changed to the modem (192.168.1.1), names resolved again.
explanation.realLife: The most common cause of the "the internet works but websites do not open" complaint is the DNS setting; especially after a modem is replaced, PCs with static settings are left pointing at the old address. To prevent it, keep PCs on DHCP whenever possible; if static settings are needed, document what was entered on which device and review that list before replacing the modem. A quick way to tell: if pinging an IP address (8.8.8.8) works but pinging a name (google.com) does not, the problem is DNS.
explanation.interviewAnswer: First I do the physical checks: is the cable plugged in, does the network icon show as connected. Then I check the IP address, mask, gateway and DNS settings with ipconfig /all. I ping the gateway and 8.8.8.8 to confirm that internet access works; when pinging google.com and nslookup fail, I know the problem is DNS. I see that the DNS server is 192.168.1.254, an address that no longer exists, correct it to the modem's address 192.168.1.1 and verify again with nslookup.

cafeGuestWifi.title: Guests can see the till

complaint.message: A customer on our guest Wi-Fi told me he could see our till from his laptop. Guests should only get internet, nothing else.

hints: From the guest laptop, ping the till (192.168.10.20) and 8.8.8.8. Both answer: the router forwards between the guest network and the office network because it has a route to both.

The fix belongs on the router, on the port the guest traffic enters (Gi0/2, 192.168.20.1). A filter there has to drop guest → office traffic but let guest → internet traffic through; the access lists card or the CLI can write it.

On the router: ip access-list extended GUEST_IN, deny ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255, permit ip any any, then on interface Gi0/2: ip access-group GUEST_IN in. Do not forget the permit line: every list ends with a hidden deny any.

explanation.whatHappened: The router had an address in both networks (192.168.10.1 office, 192.168.20.1 guests), so it routed between them like any other traffic: guests could reach the till and the office PC. Separate subnets alone do not isolate anything. An extended access list on the guest port, applied inbound, now drops packets from 192.168.20.0/24 to 192.168.10.0/24 and permits the rest, so guests still get online. For each dropped packet the router sends back an ICMP 'administratively prohibited' message.
explanation.realLife: Every café, hotel and shop that offers free Wi-Fi has to keep guests away from the till, the card terminal and the office PCs; card payment rules also expect it. Small routers often call it 'guest isolation'; on a business router you write an access list. Keep the list short, put the most specific line first, remember the implicit deny at the end and test both what must be blocked and what must still work.
explanation.interviewAnswer: I would first confirm the problem: from a guest device I ping the till and an internet address and both answer, so the router routes between the guest and office subnets. I then write an extended ACL that denies the guest subnet to the office subnet and permits everything else, and apply it inbound on the guest interface, as close to the source as possible. Finally I test again: the till must no longer answer, the guest must still reach the internet, and show access-lists must show matches on the deny line.

officeSharedIp.title: The office cannot reach the tax portal

complaint.message: The provider installed our new line yesterday and gave us a single fixed IP. Since then none of our computers can open the tax portal. The provider says the line is fine.

hints: From an office PC, ping the tax portal (198.51.100.10) and then the office router's line address (203.0.113.2): the router answers, the portal does not. Now ping the portal from the office router's own command line: it works. Ask yourself where the portal sends its answer to 192.168.1.10.

Private addresses (192.168.x.x) are not routed on the internet: the provider routes back only the single public address it gave you (203.0.113.2). The office router has to send the PCs' traffic out with that address and remember who asked: NAT with overload (PAT).

On the office router: access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255; interface Gi0/0: ip nat inside; interface Gi0/1: ip nat outside; then ip nat inside source list 1 interface Gi0/1 overload. Check with show ip nat translations after a ping.

explanation.whatHappened: The PCs' requests reached the portal with their private source address 192.168.1.x. The portal answered, but the provider's router had no route to 192.168.1.0/24 (no one on the internet has), so every answer was dropped. With PAT the office router replaces the source with its single public address 203.0.113.2 and a port number, keeps a translation table, and puts the right private address back on the answers. Now all the PCs share one public address.
explanation.realLife: Almost every small business and home network works like this: one public address from the provider, many devices behind it. Usually the provider's modem does the NAT; when the modem is put in bridge mode or replaced by your own router, the NAT has to be configured on your router. A typical sign: the router can ping the internet, the PCs cannot.
explanation.interviewAnswer: I would test step by step: the PC reaches its gateway, the router reaches the provider and the portal, but the PC does not reach the portal. That points at the return path: private addresses are not routed on the internet. I would configure PAT: an ACL that lists the inside network, ip nat inside on the LAN interface, ip nat outside on the WAN interface and ip nat inside source list … interface … overload. Then I verify with a ping and show ip nat translations, which lists each inside address with the public address and port it was given.

mallShopFirewall.title: The shop next door can see our till

complaint.from: Phone shop owner in a shopping mall
complaint.message: The shop next door told us their computer can see our till and our stock PC. Our firewall gets its line from the mall's network, where all the other shops are too. The technician who set it up last year said he 'opened it up so the card payments get their answers'. Card payments must keep working.

hints: From the neighbour's PC, ping the till (192.168.50.10) and the stock PC (192.168.50.20): both answer. Now look at the firewall: show nameif lists outside at level 0 and inside at level 100, and show running-config shows an access-group on the outside interface. What does that list let in?

A stateful firewall remembers every connection that starts on the inside (show conn) and lets its answers back in on its own. Traffic that starts on a lower level (outside) and goes to a higher one (inside) is blocked unless an access list bound to the outside interface lets it in. OUTSIDE_IN says permit ip any any: it lets every tenant in.

On the firewall: no access-group OUTSIDE_IN in interface outside (or clear the outside binding in the port settings). Then ping the payment server (10.20.0.10) from the till: it still works, and show conn lists the connection. From the neighbour's PC the shop no longer answers.

explanation.whatHappened: The firewall already did the right thing on its own: the till's requests to the payment server opened connections, and the answers came back through the connection table. The old technician's list permit ip any any, bound inbound on the outside interface, was never needed for that. What it did was turn the outside → inside rule around: with an inbound list in place, the firewall lets in whatever the list permits, and this one permitted everything. Removing the binding restores the default: inside may start connections, outside may not.
explanation.realLife: A shop in a mall, an office in a business centre or a stand at a fair often gets its line from a shared network full of strangers. 'Allow any any so it works' is one of the most common mistakes on small-business firewalls: it usually comes from a time when replies did not seem to arrive, and it quietly opens the inside to every neighbour. The fix is to rely on the connection table and to write exceptions only for services that really must be reached from outside.
explanation.interviewAnswer: I would first prove the exposure: from a host on the outside network I reach the inside hosts. On the firewall I check show nameif for the levels and the running-config for an access-group on the outside interface. A stateful firewall lets the answers to inside-initiated traffic back in through its connection table, so an inbound permit any any is never needed for that; it only opens the inside. I remove the binding (no access-group … in interface outside), then verify both sides: the till still reaches the payment server, show conn lists the connection, and the outside host can no longer reach the inside.

dmzWebsite.title: Customers cannot open our website

complaint.message: We moved our portfolio website onto our own server in the office so we stop paying for hosting. Inside the office it opens fine, but customers say the site at 203.0.113.10 does not open at all. The provider says that address is routed to our firewall.

hints: From an office PC, ping the web server (172.16.1.10): it answers. From the customer's laptop, ping 203.0.113.10: nothing answers. Look at the firewall: show nameif shows outside 0, inside 100, dmz 50. No device in the lab owns 203.0.113.10.

Two things are missing. Nothing turns the public address into the server's real address: that is static NAT. And traffic from outside (level 0) to the DMZ (level 50) goes from a lower to a higher level, so it needs an exception: an access list bound in on the outside interface. On this firewall the list names the server's real address, not the public one.

On the firewall: object network WEB_SERVER, host 172.16.1.10, nat (dmz,outside) static 203.0.113.10. Then access-list OUTSIDE_IN extended permit tcp any host 172.16.1.10 eq www, access-list OUTSIDE_IN extended permit icmp any host 172.16.1.10, and access-group OUTSIDE_IN in interface outside. Check from the customer's laptop and with show conn.

explanation.whatHappened: The provider delivered every packet for 203.0.113.10 to the firewall, but the firewall had no translation for that address and no rule that let outside traffic into the DMZ, so it dropped the packets. Static NAT now maps 203.0.113.10 to the web server's real address 172.16.1.10, and the OUTSIDE_IN list lets web traffic (and ping) to that server in from the outside. The server still cannot start connections towards the office: the DMZ (50) is lower than the inside (100), and there is no list on the DMZ interface.
explanation.realLife: This is the classic way a small business hosts its own website, mail or camera recorder: the server sits in a DMZ, reachable from the internet through one public address and only on the ports it needs, while the office network stays closed even to that server. If the server is ever broken into, the attacker is stuck in the DMZ. The same two steps (translation + exception) apply to any service you publish.
explanation.interviewAnswer: I would trace the path: the provider routes the public address to the firewall, so the packets arrive and are dropped there. Publishing a server needs two things on the firewall: a static NAT from the public address to the server's real address, and an access list bound inbound on the outside interface that permits only the needed service to the server. On current firewall software the list names the real address, because the firewall matches it after undoing the translation. I keep the DMZ at a lower level than the inside so the server cannot start connections to the office, and I verify with a test from outside and show conn.

clinicFirewallLevel.title: The clinic is offline after the firewall swap

complaint.message: Our old firewall broke on Friday and the technician installed a new one over the weekend. Since Monday morning neither the reception PC nor the doctor's PC can get online, so we cannot see appointments or send X-rays. The provider says the line is up.

hints: From the reception PC, ping the firewall's inside address (192.168.10.1): it answers. Ping 8.8.8.8: nothing. On the firewall, show nameif: compare the security level of the inside interface with the outside one.

The technician named the inside interface 'lan' instead of 'inside'. Only the name 'inside' gets level 100 automatically; any other name starts at 0. Now both interfaces have level 0, and a firewall passes nothing between two interfaces of the same level. An interface without any nameif passes nothing at all.

On the firewall: interface Gi0/1, security-level 100 (or nameif inside, which brings level 100 with it). The firewall-wide settings are locked: same-security-traffic permit inter-interface would also make it work, but it lets any equal-level interfaces talk freely. Check with show nameif and a ping to 8.8.8.8.

explanation.whatHappened: The new firewall had the right addresses and the right route, but its inside interface was named 'lan' without a security level. A name other than 'inside' starts at level 0, the same as the outside, and traffic between two interfaces of the same level is blocked by default. Giving the inside interface level 100 restores the normal order: inside (100) may start connections to outside (0), and the answers come back through the connection table.
explanation.realLife: Replacing a firewall by retyping its configuration is a typical weekend job, and a different interface name or a missing security-level line is an easy slip. The symptom is always the same: the PCs reach the firewall but nothing behind it. show nameif (or the interface table in the firewall card) shows names and levels at a glance. The same-security switch exists for real designs with several equal zones, not as a quick fix.
explanation.interviewAnswer: I would check from a PC: the gateway answers, the internet does not, so the problem is on or past the firewall. On the firewall I run show nameif: the inside interface was named 'lan' and has level 0, like outside. Equal levels do not pass traffic by default, and only the name 'inside' gets 100 automatically. I set security-level 100 on that interface rather than enabling same-security-traffic, then verify with a ping and show conn.
